14: # Cursor CLI Hook Contract
15: 
16: ---
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: Cursor 1.7+ ships a native hook system, and — unlike every sibling CLI's hooks — Cursor CLI's hooks are **the exact same hooks the Cursor editor uses**, not a CLI-private surface. There is no separate "enable hooks" feature flag to set; the hooks system is native and always active once a `hooks.json` file exists at a discovered location.
21: 
22: This packet ships its own hook adapter layer (`004-cursor-hook-adapter-layer`) and a committed, project-level registration file (`.cursor/hooks.json`, `010-cursor-hooks-live-wiring`). This reference documents the confirmed contract those adapters were built against.
23: 
24: ---
25: 
26: ## 2. REGISTRATION
27: 
28: Cursor reads hook entries from a `hooks.json` file. Schema (confirmed live against an installed `hooks.json`):
29: 
30: ```json
31: {
32:   "version": 1,
33:   "hooks": {
34:     "<event>": [
35:       {
36:         "command": "./path/to/script.sh",
37:         "timeout": 30,
38:         "type": "command",
39:         "matcher": "pattern",
40:         "loop_limit": 5,
41:         "failClosed": false
42:       }
43:     ]
44:   }
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: `command`, `timeout`, `type`, `matcher`, `loop_limit`, and `failClosed` were all observed on live entries or documented; `type` is `"command"` for a shell-executed hook.
49: 
50: ---
51: 
52: ## 3. DISCOVERY ORDER
53: 
54: Highest precedence to lowest:
55: 
56: | Scope | Path (macOS) | Path (Linux/WSL) | Path (Windows) |
57: |---|---|---|---|
58: | Enterprise | `/Library/Application Support/Cursor/hooks.json` | `/etc/cursor/hooks.json` | `C:\ProgramData\Cursor\hooks.json` |
59: | Team | Enterprise dashboard | — | — |
60: | Project | `<project-root>/.cursor/hooks.json` | same | same |
61: | User | `~/.cursor/hooks.json` | same | same |
62: 
63: Because project and user scope are the same files the Cursor **editor** reads, any hook installed here fires for both the editor and CLI sessions in this repo — see `shared-editor-config.md` for the isolation implications.
64: 
65: ---
66: 
67: ## 4. DOCUMENTED AGENT EVENTS
68: 
69: Confirmed documented event names: `sessionStart`, `sessionEnd`, `preToolUse`, `postToolUse`, `postToolUseFailure`, `subagentStart`, `subagentStop`, `beforeShellExecution`, `afterShellExecution`, `beforeMCPExecution`, `afterMCPExecution`, `beforeReadFile`, `afterFileEdit`, `beforeSubmitPrompt`, `preCompact`, `stop`, `afterAgentResponse`, `afterAgentThought` (plus Tab-completion and `workspaceOpen` app-lifecycle events that are editor-only, not agent-session events).
70: 
71: A live `~/.cursor/hooks.json` on the reference machine used `beforeSubmitPrompt`, `stop`, `beforeShellExecution`, `beforeMCPExecution`, `sessionStart`, and `sessionEnd` — confirming the schema shape live, though that particular install is user-owned tooling, not this packet's own adapter.
72: 
73: ---
74: 
75: ## 5. RESPONSE ENVELOPE
76: 
77: Command-based hooks return a JSON object on stdout:
78: 
79: ```json
80: {
81:   "permission": "allow",
82:   "user_message": "Shown to the human operator",
83:   "agent_message": "Shown to the agent/model"
84: }
85: ```
86: 
87: `permission` is `"allow"`, `"deny"`, or `"ask"`.
88: 
89: ---
90: 
91: ## 6. EXIT AND TIMEOUT SEMANTICS
92: 
93: | Condition | Behavior |
94: | --- | --- |
95: | Exit `0` | Hook succeeds; its response envelope (if any) is honored. |
96: | Exit `2` | Blocks the action the hook gated. |
97: | Other non-zero exits | Not confirmed live; treat conservatively as a hook failure until verified. |
98: | Timeout | Governed by the entry's own `timeout` field (seconds); behavior past timeout is not yet live-verified. |
99: 
100: ---
101: 
102: ## 7. PARTIAL EVENT DELIVERY (CLI VS EDITOR)
103: 
104: Live probing confirmed that Cursor CLI delivers `sessionStart`, `sessionEnd`, `preToolUse`, `postToolUse`, and `beforeMCPExecution`, but did not deliver `beforeSubmitPrompt` under the tested build. The repository therefore uses `sessionStart` for guarded spec-gate prebinding and keeps prompt classification registered only for forward compatibility. Do not treat registration alone as proof of delivery for any other event.
105: 
106: ---
107: 
108: ## 8. SOURCES
109: 
110: - Cursor hooks documentation: `cursor.com/docs/hooks`
111: - Live `~/.cursor/hooks.json` on the reference machine (schema cross-check)
112: - Community CLI-hooks-parity report: `forum.cursor.com` (unconfirmed against this specific build — verify before relying on it)

13: 
14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
199: 
200: ---
201: 
202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 3. WHEN TO CREATE REFERENCE FILES
235: 
236: ### Create Reference File When
237: 
238: **Workflow Complexity**:
239: - Multi-phase workflows with validation checkpoints
240: - Decision trees with multiple branches
241: - Pattern libraries with 5+ variations
242: - Systematic debugging procedures
243: 
244: **Technical Depth**:
245: - Root cause analysis required
246: - Tool integration details (MCP, scripts)
247: - Before/after code transformations
248: - Common error patterns and fixes
249: 
250: **Size Threshold**:
251: - Content exceeds 200 lines
252: - Multiple related workflows
253: - Extensive troubleshooting needed
254: 
255: ### Keep in SKILL.md When
256: 
257: **Core Content**:
258: - Overview and "When to Use"
259: - High-level workflow (3-5 steps)
260: - Essential rules (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)
261:   > **Note**: RULES sections in SKILL.md use ALL-CAPS H3 headers: `### ALWAYS`, `### NEVER`, `### ESCALATE IF` (or `####` at phase depth). See [skill-md-template.md](./skill-md-template.md) for the complete pattern.
262: - Quick reference
263: 
264: **Size**: Content under 200 lines
265: 
266: ### Reference File Types for AI Agent Skills
267: 
268: | Type                | Purpose                                | Example (kebab-case)          | Size           |
269: | ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------- |
270: | **Workflow**        | Multi-phase processes with checkpoints | `implementation-workflows.md` | 500-1500 lines |
271: | **Pattern Library** | Code patterns with before/after        | `shared-patterns.md`          | 300-800 lines  |
272: | **Standards**       | Rules and conventions                  | `code-quality-standards.md`   | 400-1000 lines |
273: | **Debugging**       | Systematic troubleshooting             | `debugging-workflows.md`      | 600-1200 lines |
274: | **Tool Guide**      | MCP/external tool integration          | `devtools-guide.md`           | 200-600 lines  |
275: | **Quick Reference** | Commands, shortcuts, checklists        | `quick-reference.md`          | 200-400 lines  |
276: 
277: **Note:** All authored reference file names use kebab-case (hyphens, lowercase).
278: 
279: ---
280: 
281: ## 4. AI AGENT SKILL REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS
282: 
283: ### Core Principle Statements
284: 
285: **Purpose**: Distill philosophy into one-line wisdom
286: 
287: > **PLACEMENT**: Core Principle goes in **Section 1 OVERVIEW**, NOT in the intro paragraph after the H1 title.
288: 
289: **Format**:
290: ```markdown
291: \## 1. OVERVIEW
292: 
293: ### Purpose
294: 
295: [The outcome this reference produces]
296: 
297: ### When to Use
298: 
299: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
300: 
301: ### Core Principle
302: 
303: [Single powerful statement that captures the workflow's essence]
304: ```
305: 
306: **Examples from Real Skills**:
307: - "Wait for the actual condition you care about, not a guess about how long it takes"
308: - "ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure"
309: - "Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history"
310: 
311: ### Phased Workflows with Validation
312: 
313: **Purpose**: Structured processes with mandatory checkpoints
314: 
315: **Format**:
316: ```markdown
317: ### The [Number] Phases
318: 
319: You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
320: 
321: #### Phase 1: [Phase Name]
322: 
323: **Purpose**: [What this phase accomplishes]
324: 
325: **Actions**:
326: 1. [Action 1]
327: 2. [Action 2]
328: 
329: **Validation**: `checkpoint_name`
330: 
331: #### Phase 2: [Phase Name]
332: 
333: [Similar structure]
334: ```
335: 
336: **Key Elements**:
337: - **"You MUST complete"** - Mandatory language
338: - **Named checkpoints** - `checkpoint_name` for validation
339: - **Sequential phases** - Cannot skip ahead
340: 
341: ### Before/After Code Examples
342: 
343: **Purpose**: Show transformation from wrong to right
344: 
345: **Format**:
346: ```markdown
347: ### [Pattern Name]
348: 
349: **BEFORE**: [Problem description]
350: \```[language]
351: // Bad code with issues
352: // Showing what NOT to do
353: \```
354: 
355: **AFTER**: [Solution description]
356: \```[language]
357: // Good code with fixes
358: // Showing correct approach
359: \```
360: 
361: **Why better**: [Explanation of improvement]
362: ```
363: 
364: **Key Elements**:
365: - `BEFORE:` marker for the wrong-way code
366: - `AFTER:` marker for the right-way code
367: - Inline comments explaining issues
368: - "Why better" rationale
369: 
370: ### Pattern Comparison Tables
371: 
372: **Purpose**: Compare approaches across scenarios
373: 
374: **Format**:
375: ```markdown
376: ### Common Patterns
377: 
378: | Scenario     | Approach A (Wrong) | Approach B (Right) | Why Better  |
379: | ------------ | ------------------ | ------------------ | ----------- |
380: | [Scenario 1] | [Wrong way]        | [Right way]        | [Rationale] |
381: | [Scenario 2] | [Wrong way]        | [Right way]        | [Rationale] |
382: ```
383: 
384: **Use when**: Multiple scenarios need comparison
385: 
386: ### Decision Logic in Markdown
387: 
388: **Purpose**: Explicit if/then logic for workflow decisions
389: 
390: **Format**:
391: \```markdown
392: ### Decision Logic
393: 
394: \```markdown
395: IF [condition A]:
396:   → [Action/Path A]
397:   → [Expected outcome A]
398: 
399: IF [condition B]:
400:   → [Action/Path B]
401:   → [Expected outcome B]
402: 
403: IF [condition C]:
404:   → [Action/Path C]
405:   → [Expected outcome C]
406: \```
407: \```
408: 
409: **Alternative format** (decision tree):
410: \```markdown
411: \```
412: Analyze situation
413: ├─ Condition A met
414: │  └─ Execute Workflow A
415: │     └─ Expected outcome A
416: ├─ Condition B met
417: │  └─ Execute Workflow B
418: │     └─ Expected outcome B
419: └─ Condition C met
420:    └─ Execute Workflow C
421:       └─ Expected outcome C
422: \```
423: \```
424: 
425: ### Validation Checkpoints
426: 
427: **Purpose**: Named checkpoints throughout workflows
428: 
429: **Format**:
430: ```markdown
431: **Validation**: `checkpoint_name`
432: ```
433: 
434: **Examples**:
435: - `files_analyzed`
436: - `artifacts_filtered`
437: - `strategy_determined`

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766: 
767: ---
768: 
769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882: 
883: ---
884: 
885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006: 
1007: ---
1008: 
1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"
1073:

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```

230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]

818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)

885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION

887: ### When to Use Python for Logic

889: **Use Python scripts when**:

16: # Cross-AI Orchestration Patterns: Calling AI + Cursor CLI
17: 
18: Proven patterns for orchestrating Cursor CLI from any AI assistant session.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Core Principle
25: 
26: The calling AI acts as the orchestrator (planner, validator, integrator) while Cursor CLI executes targeted tasks. The value comes from combining different model perspectives — including Cursor's own Composer model — not from redundant work.
27: 
28: ### Purpose
29: 
30: Each pattern documented here includes the rationale, implementation template, and practical considerations for combining the calling AI with Cursor CLI effectively.
31: 
32: ### When to Use
33: 
34: - You need a second AI perspective on generated code, or specifically Cursor's own Composer model's perspective
35: - You want read-only exploration (`--mode plan`/`--mode ask`) before committing to a write-capable dispatch
36: - You want to run parallel AI tasks while the calling AI continues working
37: - Complex workflows benefit from structured, multi-stage generation and validation
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## 2. GENERATE-REVIEW-FIX CYCLE
42: 
43: **The most reliable cross-AI pattern.** One AI generates, the other reviews, then the original fixes.
44: 
45: ### Flow
46: 
47: ```
48: Calling AI (plan) --> Cursor CLI (generate) --> Calling AI (review) --> Cursor CLI (fix)
49: ```
50: 
51: ### Implementation
52: 
53: ```bash
54: # Step 1: Cursor generates the code
55: cursor-agent -p \
56:   "Create a rate limiter middleware for Express with sliding window algorithm. Output only the code, no explanation." \
57:   --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled --output-format text > /tmp/rate-limiter.ts
58: 
59: # Step 2: Calling AI reviews (done within the calling AI session)
60: # Read /tmp/rate-limiter.ts, identify issues, write review to /tmp/review.md
61: 
62: # Step 3: Cursor fixes based on review
63: cursor-agent -p \
64:   "In rate-limiter.ts, fix these issues: $(cat /tmp/review.md)" \
65:   --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled --output-format text > /tmp/rate-limiter-v2.ts
66: ```
67: 
68: ### When to Use
69: 
70: - Code generation tasks where a second perspective catches edge cases
71: - Composer-specific validation, when the task specifically wants Cursor's native model's opinion
72: - Architecture decisions that benefit from adversarial review
73: 
74: ### Considerations
75: 
76: - Always validate the final output yourself (neither AI is infallible)
77: - Keep the review focused: bullet points of specific issues, not general feedback
78: - Limit to 2 fix cycles maximum; diminishing returns beyond that
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: ## 3. JSON OUTPUT PROCESSING
83: 
84: **Extract structured data from Cursor for programmatic use in the calling AI's workflows.**
85: 
86: ### Implementation
87: 
88: ```bash
89: # --output-format json gives a structured envelope: {type, result, session_id, usage, ...}
90: cursor-agent -p \
91:   "Analyze src/auth.ts and return JSON with: {functions: [{name, params, returnType}], issues: [{line, severity, description}]}" \
92:   --model composer-2.5 --sandbox enabled --output-format json > /tmp/envelope.json
93: 
94: # The model's own answer is in the .result field; parse that separately
95: jq -r '.result' /tmp/envelope.json > /tmp/analysis.json
96: jq '.issues[] | select(.severity == "high")' /tmp/analysis.json
97: ```
98: 
99: ### Output Notes
100: 
101: `--output-format json` wraps the envelope (`session_id`, `usage`, `request_id`) around the model's answer in `.result` — the model's own answer inside `.result` may still be plain text or a markdown-fenced JSON block, since Cursor has no separate schema-enforcement flag:
102: 
103: - The model may wrap its own JSON answer in a markdown code block (` ```json ... ``` `) inside `.result`
104: - Strip the code fence before parsing the inner content with `jq`/`JSON.parse`
105: - Use explicit prompt instructions: "Return only raw JSON with no explanation or code fences."
106: 
107: ### When to Use
108: 
109: - Extracting metrics, function signatures, or dependency lists
110: - Feeding Cursor analysis into the calling AI's decision logic
111: - Building automated pipelines that branch on structured output, or that need the `session_id` for a later `--resume`
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 4. BACKGROUND EXECUTION
116: 
117: **Run Cursor tasks in parallel while the calling AI continues working.**
118: 
119: ### Implementation
120: 
121: ```bash
122: # Launch multiple Cursor tasks in background
123: cursor-agent -p "Review src/api/ for issues. Return JSON." \
124:   --model composer-2.5 --sandbox enabled --output-format text > /tmp/review.txt 2>&1 &
125: PID1=$!
126: 
127: cursor-agent -p "Generate unit tests for src/utils.ts" \
128:   --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled --output-format text > /tmp/generated-tests.ts 2>&1 &
129: PID2=$!
130: 
131: # Calling AI continues other work...
132: 
133: # Wait for specific task
134: wait $PID1
135: echo "Review complete"
136: cat /tmp/review.txt | head -20
137: 
138: # Wait for all
139: wait $PID1 $PID2
140: echo "All Cursor tasks complete"
141: ```
142: 
143: ### Considerations
144: 
145: - Always redirect stderr: `2>&1` to capture errors alongside output
146: - Set reasonable timeouts: `timeout 120 cursor-agent -p ...` to prevent hung processes
147: - Do not background two write-capable dispatches that touch the same files (race conditions)
148: - Background read-only (`--mode ask`/`--mode plan`) tasks are safe to parallelize freely
149: 
150: ### Silent Stdin Consumption When Dispatching in a `while read` Loop
151: 
152: The same class of bug that affects other backgrounded CLI dispatches applies here: when a dispatcher script iterates over lines of input with `while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < input.jsonl` and launches `cursor-agent -p ... &` inside the loop body, the backgrounded process can inherit the loop's stdin and race the `read` command for lines, silently dropping most dispatches.
153: 
154: ```bash
155: # RISKY: cursor-agent may inherit the loop's stdin
156: while IFS= read -r line; do
157:   cursor-agent -p "$PROMPT" --model composer-2.5 --sandbox enabled > "$LOG" 2>&1 &
158:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
159: done < input.jsonl
160: 
161: # SAFE: redirect cursor-agent stdin from /dev/null so the loop keeps its own
162: while IFS= read -r line; do
163:   cursor-agent -p "$PROMPT" --model composer-2.5 --sandbox enabled > "$LOG" 2>&1 </dev/null &
164:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
165: done < input.jsonl
166: ```
167: 
168: **Always pair `cursor-agent -p ... &` inside a read-loop with `</dev/null` on the redirection.** Live-verified: a `cursor-agent -p ... </dev/null` dispatch completes normally with no hang, confirming the redirection is safe and does not interfere with the CLI's own operation.

172: ## 5. MODEL SELECTION STRATEGY
173: 
174: **cli-cursor dispatch is scoped to an enforced 29-id allowlist — Composer, Gemini 3.8 Flash High, GLM 5.2, GPT-5.6 Luna Max, and Grok (4.5, 4.6 and 4.7) only. Choose based on task type; never dispatch a model outside this set.**
175: 
176: ### Decision Matrix
177: 
178: | Task Type | Model choice | Rationale |
179: |-----------|-----------------|-----------|
180: | General delegation | `composer-2.5` (default) | Cursor's own model; predictable, always allowed |
181: | Task specifically wants Cursor's own model | `composer-2.5` / `composer-2.5-fast` | Cursor-exclusive — no hosted-provider equivalent |
182: | Architecture / security analysis at high or extra-high depth | `cursor-grok-4.6-high` / `-xhigh` (or `-fast` siblings), or `glm-5.2-max` | Effort is baked into the id; pick the high or xhigh tier — 4.6's xhigh is the deepest available |
183: | Code generation | `composer-2.5`, or `cursor-grok-4.5-medium` / `cursor-grok-4.6-medium` | Balanced for most generation tasks |
184: | Trivial lookups | `composer-2.5-fast` | The fast variant is quicker for simple tasks |
185: | Task wants a model NOT on this list (e.g. GPT, Claude, Gemini, Kimi via Cursor) | **Not supported by this skill** | Escalate to the user rather than substituting an allowed model silently |
186: 
187: ### Implementation
188:

191: cursor-agent -p "Add error handling to auth.ts" --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled
192: 
193: # Composer-specific request
194: cursor-agent -p "Review this diff for correctness" --model composer-2.5 --sandbox enabled
195: 
196: # High-effort analysis — pick the tier via the id itself, not a flag
197: cursor-agent -p "Review the authentication architecture for security gaps" \
198:   --mode ask --model cursor-grok-4.6-high
199: 
200: # NEVER: parameterized bracket syntax — rejected outright by the live CLI
201: # cursor-agent -p "..." --model 'cursor-grok-4.6[effort=high]'   # "Cannot use this model"
202: 
203: # NEVER: a model outside the enforced allowlist, including auto

205: # cursor-agent -p "..." --model gpt-5.6-sol-high-fast  # not on the allowlist at all
206: ```
207: 
208: ### Why Explicit Model Specification Matters
209: 
210: - Omitting `--model` defaults to `composer-2.5`, never `auto` — the runtime layer rejects `auto` outright since it can silently resolve outside the allowlist
211: - Explicit specification ensures reproducible behavior in scripts and CI/CD pipelines
212: - The allowlist is fixed at 29 ids (`executor-config.ts`'s `CURSOR_SUPPORTED_MODELS`) — do not query `cursor-agent --list-models` to justify dispatching an id outside it; that command lists Cursor's full roster, not this skill's scope

218: **Choose the least-permissive approval/sandbox combination that allows the task to succeed.**

223: Task type?

225:   +-- Analysis / exploration / Q&A --> --mode ask or --mode plan (read-only regardless of approval flags)
226:   |

15: 
16: # Cross-AI Orchestration Patterns: Calling AI + Cursor CLI
17: 
18: Proven patterns for orchestrating Cursor CLI from any AI assistant session.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Core Principle
25: 
26: The calling AI acts as the orchestrator (planner, validator, integrator) while Cursor CLI executes targeted tasks. The value comes from combining different model perspectives — including Cursor's own Composer model — not from redundant work.
27: 
28: ### Purpose
29: 
30: Each pattern documented here includes the rationale, implementation template, and practical considerations for combining the calling AI with Cursor CLI effectively.
31: 
32: ### When to Use
33: 
34: - You need a second AI perspective on generated code, or specifically Cursor's own Composer model's perspective
35: - You want read-only exploration (`--mode plan`/`--mode ask`) before committing to a write-capable dispatch
36: - You want to run parallel AI tasks while the calling AI continues working
37: - Complex workflows benefit from structured, multi-stage generation and validation
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## 2. GENERATE-REVIEW-FIX CYCLE
42: 
43: **The most reliable cross-AI pattern.** One AI generates, the other reviews, then the original fixes.
44: 
45: ### Flow
46: 
47: ```
48: Calling AI (plan) --> Cursor CLI (generate) --> Calling AI (review) --> Cursor CLI (fix)
49: ```
50: 
51: ### Implementation
52: 
53: ```bash
54: # Step 1: Cursor generates the code
55: cursor-agent -p \
56:   "Create a rate limiter middleware for Express with sliding window algorithm. Output only the code, no explanation." \
57:   --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled --output-format text > /tmp/rate-limiter.ts
58: 
59: # Step 2: Calling AI reviews (done within the calling AI session)
60: # Read /tmp/rate-limiter.ts, identify issues, write review to /tmp/review.md
61: 
62: # Step 3: Cursor fixes based on review
63: cursor-agent -p \
64:   "In rate-limiter.ts, fix these issues: $(cat /tmp/review.md)" \
65:   --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled --output-format text > /tmp/rate-limiter-v2.ts
66: ```
67: 
68: ### When to Use
69: 
70: - Code generation tasks where a second perspective catches edge cases
71: - Composer-specific validation, when the task specifically wants Cursor's native model's opinion
72: - Architecture decisions that benefit from adversarial review
73: 
74: ### Considerations
75: 
76: - Always validate the final output yourself (neither AI is infallible)
77: - Keep the review focused: bullet points of specific issues, not general feedback
78: - Limit to 2 fix cycles maximum; diminishing returns beyond that
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: ## 3. JSON OUTPUT PROCESSING
83: 
84: **Extract structured data from Cursor for programmatic use in the calling AI's workflows.**
85: 
86: ### Implementation
87: 
88: ```bash
89: # --output-format json gives a structured envelope: {type, result, session_id, usage, ...}
90: cursor-agent -p \
91:   "Analyze src/auth.ts and return JSON with: {functions: [{name, params, returnType}], issues: [{line, severity, description}]}" \
92:   --model composer-2.5 --sandbox enabled --output-format json > /tmp/envelope.json
93: 
94: # The model's own answer is in the .result field; parse that separately
95: jq -r '.result' /tmp/envelope.json > /tmp/analysis.json
96: jq '.issues[] | select(.severity == "high")' /tmp/analysis.json
97: ```
98: 
99: ### Output Notes
100: 
101: `--output-format json` wraps the envelope (`session_id`, `usage`, `request_id`) around the model's answer in `.result` — the model's own answer inside `.result` may still be plain text or a markdown-fenced JSON block, since Cursor has no separate schema-enforcement flag:
102: 
103: - The model may wrap its own JSON answer in a markdown code block (` ```json ... ``` `) inside `.result`
104: - Strip the code fence before parsing the inner content with `jq`/`JSON.parse`
105: - Use explicit prompt instructions: "Return only raw JSON with no explanation or code fences."
106: 
107: ### When to Use
108: 
109: - Extracting metrics, function signatures, or dependency lists
110: - Feeding Cursor analysis into the calling AI's decision logic
111: - Building automated pipelines that branch on structured output, or that need the `session_id` for a later `--resume`
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 4. BACKGROUND EXECUTION
116: 
117: **Run Cursor tasks in parallel while the calling AI continues working.**
118: 
119: ### Implementation
120: 
121: ```bash
122: # Launch multiple Cursor tasks in background
123: cursor-agent -p "Review src/api/ for issues. Return JSON." \
124:   --model composer-2.5 --sandbox enabled --output-format text > /tmp/review.txt 2>&1 &
125: PID1=$!
126: 
127: cursor-agent -p "Generate unit tests for src/utils.ts" \
128:   --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled --output-format text > /tmp/generated-tests.ts 2>&1 &
129: PID2=$!
130: 
131: # Calling AI continues other work...
132: 
133: # Wait for specific task
134: wait $PID1
135: echo "Review complete"
136: cat /tmp/review.txt | head -20
137: 
138: # Wait for all
139: wait $PID1 $PID2
140: echo "All Cursor tasks complete"
141: ```
142: 
143: ### Considerations
144: 
145: - Always redirect stderr: `2>&1` to capture errors alongside output
146: - Set reasonable timeouts: `timeout 120 cursor-agent -p ...` to prevent hung processes
147: - Do not background two write-capable dispatches that touch the same files (race conditions)
148: - Background read-only (`--mode ask`/`--mode plan`) tasks are safe to parallelize freely
149: 
150: ### Silent Stdin Consumption When Dispatching in a `while read` Loop
151: 
152: The same class of bug that affects other backgrounded CLI dispatches applies here: when a dispatcher script iterates over lines of input with `while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < input.jsonl` and launches `cursor-agent -p ... &` inside the loop body, the backgrounded process can inherit the loop's stdin and race the `read` command for lines, silently dropping most dispatches.
153: 
154: ```bash
155: # RISKY: cursor-agent may inherit the loop's stdin
156: while IFS= read -r line; do
157:   cursor-agent -p "$PROMPT" --model composer-2.5 --sandbox enabled > "$LOG" 2>&1 &
158:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
159: done < input.jsonl
160: 
161: # SAFE: redirect cursor-agent stdin from /dev/null so the loop keeps its own
162: while IFS= read -r line; do
163:   cursor-agent -p "$PROMPT" --model composer-2.5 --sandbox enabled > "$LOG" 2>&1 </dev/null &
164:   echo "$!" > "pid-$LINE_ID.pid"
165: done < input.jsonl
166: ```
167: 
168: **Always pair `cursor-agent -p ... &` inside a read-loop with `</dev/null` on the redirection.** Live-verified: a `cursor-agent -p ... </dev/null` dispatch completes normally with no hang, confirming the redirection is safe and does not interfere with the CLI's own operation.
169: 
170: ---
171: 
172: ## 5. MODEL SELECTION STRATEGY
173: 
174: **cli-cursor dispatch is scoped to an enforced 29-id allowlist — Composer, Gemini 3.8 Flash High, GLM 5.2, GPT-5.6 Luna Max, and Grok (4.5, 4.6 and 4.7) only. Choose based on task type; never dispatch a model outside this set.**
175: 
176: ### Decision Matrix
177: 
178: | Task Type | Model choice | Rationale |
179: |-----------|-----------------|-----------|
180: | General delegation | `composer-2.5` (default) | Cursor's own model; predictable, always allowed |
181: | Task specifically wants Cursor's own model | `composer-2.5` / `composer-2.5-fast` | Cursor-exclusive — no hosted-provider equivalent |
182: | Architecture / security analysis at high or extra-high depth | `cursor-grok-4.6-high` / `-xhigh` (or `-fast` siblings), or `glm-5.2-max` | Effort is baked into the id; pick the high or xhigh tier — 4.6's xhigh is the deepest available |
183: | Code generation | `composer-2.5`, or `cursor-grok-4.5-medium` / `cursor-grok-4.6-medium` | Balanced for most generation tasks |
184: | Trivial lookups | `composer-2.5-fast` | The fast variant is quicker for simple tasks |
185: | Task wants a model NOT on this list (e.g. GPT, Claude, Gemini, Kimi via Cursor) | **Not supported by this skill** | Escalate to the user rather than substituting an allowed model silently |
186: 
187: ### Implementation
188: 
189: ```bash
190: # General delegation — the skill default
191: cursor-agent -p "Add error handling to auth.ts" --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled
192: 
193: # Composer-specific request
194: cursor-agent -p "Review this diff for correctness" --model composer-2.5 --sandbox enabled
195: 
196: # High-effort analysis — pick the tier via the id itself, not a flag
197: cursor-agent -p "Review the authentication architecture for security gaps" \
198:   --mode ask --model cursor-grok-4.6-high
199: 
200: # NEVER: parameterized bracket syntax — rejected outright by the live CLI
201: # cursor-agent -p "..." --model 'cursor-grok-4.6[effort=high]'   # "Cannot use this model"
202: 
203: # NEVER: a model outside the enforced allowlist, including auto
204: # cursor-agent -p "..." --model auto            # rejected by fanout-run.cjs / dispatch-model.cjs
205: # cursor-agent -p "..." --model gpt-5.6-sol-high-fast  # not on the allowlist at all
206: ```
207: 
208: ### Why Explicit Model Specification Matters
209: 
210: - Omitting `--model` defaults to `composer-2.5`, never `auto` — the runtime layer rejects `auto` outright since it can silently resolve outside the allowlist
211: - Explicit specification ensures reproducible behavior in scripts and CI/CD pipelines
212: - The allowlist is fixed at 29 ids (`executor-config.ts`'s `CURSOR_SUPPORTED_MODELS`) — do not query `cursor-agent --list-models` to justify dispatching an id outside it; that command lists Cursor's full roster, not this skill's scope
213: 
214: ---
215: 
216: ## 6. APPROVAL AND SANDBOX STRATEGY
217: 
218: **Choose the least-permissive approval/sandbox combination that allows the task to succeed.**
219: 
220: ### Decision Flow
221: 
222: ```
223: Task type?
224:   |
225:   +-- Analysis / exploration / Q&A --> --mode ask or --mode plan (read-only regardless of approval flags)
226:   |
227:   +-- Code generation / refactoring --> default agent mode + --auto-review + --sandbox enabled
228:   |
229:   +-- Fully unattended run --> default agent mode + --force + --sandbox disabled
230:                                 (explicit user approval required)
231: ```
232: 
233: ### Implementation by Task Type
234: 
235: ```bash
236: # Analysis: read-only, no approval flags needed (mode itself is read-only)
237: cursor-agent -p "Identify all N+1 query patterns in src/" --mode ask --model composer-2.5
238: 
239: # Code generation: default agent + Smart Auto
240: cursor-agent -p "Add retry logic to all API calls in src/api/" \
241:   --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled
242: 
243: # Fully unattended: explicit user approval required beforehand
244: cursor-agent -p "Run the test suite and fix failures" \
245:   --model composer-2.5 --force --sandbox disabled
246: ```
247: 
248: ### Combinations to Avoid
249: 
250: | Combination | Risk | Better Approach |
251: |-------------|------|-----------------|
252: | `--force --sandbox disabled` without explicit user approval | Unrestricted, unreviewed changes | Require explicit approval before this combination; default to `--auto-review` |
253: | Two write-capable dispatches backgrounded against the same files | Race condition | Use `--mode ask`/`--mode plan` for parallel background tasks |
254: | `--auto-review` for pure exploration | Unnecessary write capability | Use `--mode ask`/`--mode plan`; they are read-only regardless of approval flags |
255: 
256: ---
257: 
258: ## 7. CONTEXT ENRICHMENT
259: 
260: **Provide Cursor with rich context for better results.**
261: 
262: ### Explicit Context Injection
263: 
264: ```bash
265: # Inject the calling AI's analysis as context

267: is not being rotated on use, allowing token replay attacks."
268:

272: ```
273: 
274: ### Project Rules (automatic, not opt-in)
275: 
276: Unlike sibling CLIs that need an explicit context file reference, Cursor CLI automatically reads `.cursor/rules`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and legacy `.cursorrules` at the project root — a dispatched session in this repo already has `AGENTS.md` loaded without any extra flag. Do not duplicate that content in the delegation prompt.
277: 
278: ### Spec-Folder Pre-Approval
279: 
280: ```bash

282:   "Spec folder: specs/cli-external-orchestration/030-cli-cursor-creation (pre-approved, skip Gate 3). \
283:    Implement the change described in tasks.md T004." \
284:   --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled
285: ```

287: ---

291: **Multi-stage validation of Cursor-generated output.**
292: 
293: ### Implementation

95: Dispatch this mode's default without opening any other file:

117: ## 4. REASONING-EFFORT / THINKING LEVER
118: 
119: **cli-cursor has NO separate effort flag.** There is no `--reasoning-effort`, no `--effort`, no `--variant`, and no `model[effort=...]` parameterized bracket. Effort is BAKED INTO the id suffix — you select a tier by choosing the exact enumerated id that carries it.
120: 
121: | Family | How to select effort | Available tiers (as id suffixes) |
122: |--------|----------------------|----------------------------------|
123: | Composer | No tier suffix; `-fast` is a latency variant, not an effort tier | `composer-2.5`, `composer-2.5-fast` |
124: | Gemini 3.8 | Pick the exact tiered id; only High is curated in-scope | `gemini-3.8-flash-high` |
125: | GLM 5.2 | Pick the exact tiered id | `-high`, `-max` |
126: | GPT-5.6 Luna | Only the Max tier is curated in-scope; `-fast` is the low-latency variant | `gpt-5.6-luna-max`, `gpt-5.6-luna-max-fast` |
127: | Grok 4.5 | Pick the exact id with the desired tier suffix (each has a `-fast` sibling) | `-low`, `-low-fast`, `-medium`, `-medium-fast`, `-high`, `-high-fast` |
128: | Grok 4.6 | Pick the exact id with the desired tier suffix (each has a `-fast` sibling) — adds `xhigh` beyond 4.5 | `-low`, `-low-fast`, `-medium`, `-medium-fast`, `-high`, `-high-fast`, `-xhigh`, `-xhigh-fast` |
129: | Grok 4.7 | Pick the exact id with the desired tier suffix (each has a `-fast` sibling). The ids carry no `cursor-` prefix | `-low`, `-low-fast`, `-medium`, `-medium-fast`, `-high`, `-high-fast`, `-xhigh`, `-xhigh-fast` |
130:

Use `cursor-grok-4.6-high`, never `cursor-grok-4.6[effort=high]`.
132: 
133: **"Max Mode" = the `-max` id, where a model offers one.** Cursor's Max Mode (the 1M-context tier) is exposed as an enumerated `-max` model id — in this allowlist `glm-5.2-max` and `gpt-5.6-luna-max` (the wider roster's `claude-*-max` / `gpt-5.6-sol-max` are out of scope). It is NOT reachable via the `[context=1m]` bracket the CLI `--help` advertises — that bracket is rejected (above). **Composer 2.5 has no `-max` variant:** `--list-models` offers only `composer-2.5` and `composer-2.5-fast`, and `composer-2.5[context=1m]` returns `Cannot use this model` — so there is no Composer Max Mode on the CLI.
134: 
135: **Id-form footgun.** The CLI-facing ids are DOTTED (`glm-5.2-high`, `glm-5.2-max`, `composer-2.5`) and are what you pass to `--model`. The deep-loop runtime's INTERNAL model uids use dashes instead (`glm-5-2` = "GLM-5.2 High", `glm-5-2-max` = "GLM-5.2 Max"). Do not pass an internal dash-form uid to `cursor-agent --model`, and do not pass a CLI dotted id where the runtime expects its uid — the two namespaces are not interchangeable.

139: ## 5. HOW TO INVOKE
140: 
141: ### Canonical dispatch shape
142: ```bash
143: cursor-agent -p --model composer-2.5 "<prompt>"
144: ```
145: 
146: ### Dispatch envelope (child / detached sessions)
147: When dispatching as a non-interactive child (spec-gate-neutralized worker), prefix the shared env and terminate stdin:
148: 
149: ```bash
150: SYSTEM_SPEC_GATE_ENFORCE=0 AI_SESSION_CHILD=1 cursor-agent -p \
151:   --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled --output-format text \
152:   "<prompt>" </dev/null > stdout.log 2> stderr.log
153: ```
154: 
155: - `SYSTEM_SPEC_GATE_ENFORCE=0 AI_SESSION_CHILD=1` — neutralizes the spec-gate for a bound child worker so it does not stall waiting on an interactive Gate-3 answer, and marks the dispatch as an orchestrated sub-session that SHARES the parent worktree (distinct from Cursor's own native `-w` worktree flag).
156: - `</dev/null` — pair with `cursor-agent -p ... &` inside a `while read` loop so the backgrounded process cannot race the loop for stdin lines. See [integration-patterns.md](./integration-patterns.md) §4.
157: 
158: ### Parallel / fan-out
159: Multi-lineage parallel dispatch is driven by `fanout-run.cjs` (executor kind `cli-cursor`), which lives outside this hub — see §6. The runtime is the single Cursor execution adapter; do not build a packet-local wrapper.

89: **Grok 4.7 joins Grok 4.5 and 4.6 (2026-09-26).** All 8 Grok 4.7 ids were confirmed in the live `cursor-agent models` list and dispatch-tested end to end on 2026-09-26 with `cursor-agent 2026.09.26-dd393fe`, and each returned a live model response with exit 0. 90: 
91: ---
92: 
93: ## 3. DEFAULTS & QUICK INVOCATION
94: 
95: Dispatch this mode's default without opening any other file:
96: 
97: | Field | Value |
98: |-------|-------|
99: | Default model | `composer-2.5` |
100: | Default effort | baked into the id (Composer has no tier suffix; the default carries no `-low/-medium/-high`) |
101: | Default approval | `--auto-review` (Smart Auto) |
102: | Default sandbox | `--sandbox enabled` |
103: | Default format | `--output-format text` |
104: 
105: ```bash
106: cursor-agent -p "<prompt>" \
107:   --model composer-2.5 \
108:   --auto-review \
109:   --sandbox enabled \
110:   --output-format text
111: ```
112: 
113: If Cursor is not authenticated, the mode ASKS the operator to run `cursor-agent login` — it never silently swaps a model. 114: 
115: ---
116: 
117: ## 4. REASONING-EFFORT / THINKING LEVER
118: 
119: **cli-cursor has NO separate effort flag.** There is no `--reasoning-effort`, no `--effort`, no `--variant`, and no `model[effort=...]` parameterized bracket. Effort is BAKED INTO the id suffix — you select a tier by choosing the exact enumerated id that carries it.
120: 
121: | Family | How to select effort | Available tiers (as id suffixes) |
122: |--------|----------------------|----------------------------------|
123: | Composer | No tier suffix; `-fast` is a latency variant, not an effort tier | `composer-2.5`, `composer-2.5-fast` |
124: | Gemini 3.8 | Pick the exact tiered id; only High is curated in-scope | `gemini-3.8-flash-high` |
125: | GLM 5.2 | Pick the exact tiered id | `-high`, `-max` |
126: | GPT-5.6 Luna | Only the Max tier is curated in-scope; `-fast` is the low-latency variant | `gpt-5.6-luna-max`, `gpt-5.6-luna-max-fast` |
127: | Grok 4.5 | Pick the exact id with the desired tier suffix (each has a `-fast` sibling) | `-low`, `-low-fast`, `-medium`, `-medium-fast`, `-high`, `-high-fast` |
128: | Grok 4.6 | Pick the exact id with the desired tier suffix (each has a `-fast` sibling) — adds `xhigh` beyond 4.5 | `-low`, `-low-fast`, `-medium`, `-medium-fast`, `-high`, `-high-fast`, `-xhigh`, `-xhigh-fast` |
129: | Grok 4.7 | Pick the exact id with the desired tier suffix (each has a `-fast` sibling). The ids carry no `cursor-` prefix | `-low`, `-low-fast`, `-medium`, `-medium-fast`, `-high`, `-high-fast`, `-xhigh`, `-xhigh-fast` |
130: 
131: **Bracket syntax is rejected outright by the CLI.** Live-tested against installed `cursor-agent 2026.07.23-e383d2b` with `composer-2.5[effort=high]`, Cursor's own `--help` example (`claude-opus-4-8[context=1m,effort=high,fast=false]`), and `cursor-grok-4.5[effort=high]`; each returned `Cannot use this model: ...` with exit 1 before repository dispatch code runs. 132: 
133: **"Max Mode" = the `-max` id, where a model offers one.** Cursor's Max Mode (the 1M-context tier) is exposed as an enumerated `-max` model id — in this allowlist `glm-5.2-max` and `gpt-5.6-luna-max` (the wider roster's `claude-*-max` / `gpt-5.6-sol-max` are out of scope). 134: 
135: **Id-form footgun.** The CLI-facing ids are DOTTED (`glm-5.2-high`, `glm-5.2-max`, `composer-2.5`) and are what you pass to `--model`. Do not pass an internal dash-form uid to `cursor-agent --model`, and do not pass a CLI dotted id where the runtime expects its uid — the two namespaces are not interchangeable.
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## 5. HOW TO INVOKE
140: 
141: ### Canonical dispatch shape
142: ```bash
143: cursor-agent -p --model composer-2.5 "<prompt>"
144: ```
145: 
146: ### Dispatch envelope (child / detached sessions)
147: When dispatching as a non-interactive child (spec-gate-neutralized worker), prefix the shared env and terminate stdin:
148: 
149: ```bash
150: SYSTEM_SPEC_GATE_ENFORCE=0 AI_SESSION_CHILD=1 cursor-agent -p \
151:   --model composer-2.5 --auto-review --sandbox enabled --output-format text \
152:   "<prompt>" </dev/null > stdout.log 2> stderr.log
153: ```
154: 
155: - `SYSTEM_SPEC_GATE_ENFORCE=0 AI_SESSION_CHILD=1` — neutralizes the spec-gate for a bound child worker so it does not stall waiting on an interactive Gate-3 answer, and marks the dispatch as an orchestrated sub-session that SHARES the parent worktree (distinct from Cursor's own native `-w` worktree flag).

157: 
158: ### Parallel / fan-out
159: Multi-lineage parallel dispatch is driven by `fanout-run.cjs` (executor kind `cli-cursor`), which lives outside this hub — see §6. The runtime is the single Cursor execution adapter; do not build a packet-local wrapper.
160: 
161: ---
162: 
163: ## 6. ENFORCEMENT & PROFILES (authoritative elsewhere — do not duplicate here)
164: 
165: - **Allowlist enforcement (source of truth)** → `CURSOR_SUPPORTED_MODELS` / `isCursorModelAllowed` in [../../../system-deep-loop/runtime/lib/deep-loop/executor-config.ts](../../../system-deep-loop/runtime/lib/deep-loop/executor-config.ts). 167: - **Live full roster** → `cursor-agent --list-models` on the target install (NOT this skill's scope)
168:

15: # Cursor CLI Shared Editor Config Surface
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Core Principle
22: 
23: Every sibling CLI in this hub keeps a tool-private config namespace: Codex reads `.codex/`, Claude Code reads `.claude/`, OpenCode reads `.opencode/`. **Cursor CLI is the one exception.** It reads the exact same config files the Cursor **editor** reads — there is no CLI-private config directory. This is the single biggest architectural difference between `cli-cursor` and its siblings, and it shapes both this packet's hook-adapter design (`004-cursor-hook-adapter-layer`, a later phase) and any dispatch-isolation decision.
24: 
25: ### Why This Matters for Orchestrated Delegation
26: 
27: A dispatched `cursor-agent -p` session run by this packet silently inherits whatever hooks, MCP servers, and rules the operator's Cursor editor already has configured on this machine — because they are, literally, the same files. An orchestrator expecting a clean, isolated CLI session (the assumption every sibling CLI safely supports) will be surprised here unless this surface is understood up front.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. DIRECTORY LAYOUT
32: 
33: ### Project Scope: `<repo-root>/.cursor/`
34: 
35: | File | Purpose |
36: |---|---|
37: | `mcp.json` | MCP server configuration |
38: | `hooks.json` | Hook registrations (see `hook-contract.md`) |
39: | `rules/` | Project-level rule files, read automatically |
40: | `worktrees.json` | Setup scripts for native worktree isolation (`-w`) |
41: 
42: ### User Scope: `~/.cursor/`
43: 
44: | File/dir | Purpose |
45: |---|---|
46: | `mcp.json` | User-level MCP server configuration |
47: | `hooks.json` | User-level hook registrations |
48: | `plugins/` | Installed plugins (see `cursor-tools.md`) |
49: | `skills-cursor/` | Cursor's own skill/subagent system |
50: | `cli-config.json` | CLI-specific settings: `version`, `editor`, `hasChangedDefaultModel`, `permissions`, `approvalMode`, `sandbox`, `network` (key names confirmed live; values were never read, to avoid surfacing stored auth material) |
51: | `worktrees/<reponame>/<name>/` | Native worktree checkouts (`-w`) |
52: 
53: ### Precedence
54: 
55: `"project → global → nested"` — a project-scoped file overrides a global (user-scoped) one, and a more deeply nested config overrides a less-nested one, matching the discovery order documented in `hook-contract.md` §3 for hooks specifically.
56: 
57: ---
58: 
59: ## 3. RULE SOURCES (READ AUTOMATICALLY)
60: 
61: Beyond `.cursor/rules`, Cursor CLI also reads project-root `AGENTS.md`, project-root `CLAUDE.md`, and legacy `.cursorrules` — all automatically, with no flag required. This repo already has an `AGENTS.md` at its root; a `cursor-agent` dispatch run here would apply it as rules without any extra configuration. This is a genuine convenience (no duplicate context injection needed, unlike a CLI that requires an explicit `@file` or context-file reference) but also means the delegation prompt does not need to (and should not) re-paste `AGENTS.md` content — see `SKILL.md` rule 11.
62: 
63: ---
64: 
65: ## 4. DISPATCH-ISOLATION IMPLICATIONS
66: 
67: ### The Core Tension
68: 
69: Every sibling CLI's dispatch is, by construction, isolated from the operator's own interactive sessions with that same tool — a dispatched `codex exec` does not inherit the operator's interactively-configured Codex TUI state in any surprising way, because Codex's config is itself scoped per-invocation via `-c` overrides and `--profile`. Cursor's shared-with-the-editor surface breaks that assumption: a dispatched `cursor-agent -p` and the operator's own open Cursor editor window read literally the same `hooks.json`/`mcp.json`/rules.
70: 
71: ### Confirmed Mitigations Available
72: 
73: | Flag | Effect | Confirmed |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `--workspace <path>` | Sets the workspace root explicitly | Yes, documented in `--help` |
76: | `--add-dir <path>` | Adds an additional accessible directory | Yes, documented in `--help` |
77: | `--plugin-dir <path>` | Adds a plugin search directory, separate from the default `~/.cursor/plugins/` | Yes, documented in `--help` |
78: 
79: ### Open Question — Not Yet Resolved
80: 
81: Whether a dispatched `cursor-agent` should carry an explicit `--workspace`/config-isolation flag combination so it does not silently inherit the operator's shared `~/.cursor/` hooks/MCP/rules is an open question, deferred to the dispatch-command finalization (tracked in `030-cli-cursor-creation/spec.md` §4 and this phase's own `spec.md` §12). This reference documents the mitigation flags that exist; it does not assert a specific isolation policy has been decided or implemented, because none has as of this packet's authoring.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ## 5. PRACTICAL GUIDANCE FOR THIS PACKET'S DELEGATIONS
86: 
87: 1. **Assume shared state by default.** Do not assume a dispatched `cursor-agent -p` session starts from a clean slate the way a dispatched `codex exec` or `claude -p` does.
88: 2. **Do not silently rely on the operator's hooks firing.** Since hook delivery under the CLI is not yet confirmed per-event (`hook-contract.md` §7), never assume a shared hook will guard a dispatch the way it might guard the operator's interactive editor session.
89: 3. **Do not re-inject `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` content into delegation prompts.** Cursor CLI already reads them automatically; duplicating that content wastes tokens and risks drift between the injected copy and the live file.
90: 4. **Treat MCP servers as shared, not dispatch-scoped.** A dispatched task using `--approve-mcps` approves whatever is configured in the (shared) `mcp.json` — the operator's editor session and this packet's dispatch draw from the same server list.
91: 
92: ---
93: 
94: ## 6. COMPARISON WITH SIBLING CLIS
95: 
96: | Aspect | `cli-codex` | `cli-claude-code` | `cli-opencode` | `cli-cursor` |
97: |---|---|---|---|---|
98: | Config directory | `.codex/` (tool-private) | `.claude/` (tool-private) | `.opencode/` (tool-private) | `.cursor/`/`~/.cursor/` (shared with editor) |
99: | Hooks shared with an editor product? | No | No | No | **Yes** — identical files |
100: | MCP config shared with an editor product? | No | No | No | **Yes** — identical files |
101: | Per-dispatch config isolation | `-c` overrides + `--profile` scope the invocation | `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` env override | `--dir`/home env override | `--workspace`/`--add-dir`/`--plugin-dir` (narrower than a full config-dir override) |
102: 
103: This table exists to make the asymmetry legible at a glance: every sibling CLI's dispatch isolation story is "point it at a different config directory." Cursor's is "there is one config surface, and you can widen or narrow what the dispatch sees, but you cannot fully redirect it to an alternate config root the way `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` does."
104: 
105: ---
106: 
107: ## 7. TROUBLESHOOTING SURPRISES TRACED TO THE SHARED SURFACE
108: 
109: | Symptom | Root cause | Where to look |
110: |---|---|---|
111: | A dispatch behaves differently than an identical prompt did yesterday | The operator changed `~/.cursor/cli-config.json` (`permissions`/`approvalMode`/`sandbox`) through the editor, and the CLI picked it up | `~/.cursor/cli-config.json` |
112: | An unexpected hook fires during an orchestrated dispatch | A hook registered for the operator's interactive editor sessions also matches the CLI's event stream | `.cursor/hooks.json` / `~/.cursor/hooks.json` — see `hook-contract.md` |
113: | A dispatch has access to an MCP server nobody configured for this task | The server was configured for the operator's editor sessions and is shared | `.cursor/mcp.json` / `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |
114: | A dispatch applies a rule the delegation prompt never mentioned | `.cursor/rules`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, or `.cursorrules` applied automatically | §3 above |
115: | Model roster looks different across two machines | `~/.cursor/cli-config.json`'s `hasChangedDefaultModel` and account-level settings differ per machine/account | `cursor-agent about` / `--list-models` |
116: 
117: Each of these is expected, documented behavior once this reference is read — not a bug in `cli-cursor`'s dispatch adapter. Attribute a surprising dispatch outcome here before assuming the adapter itself misbehaved.
